29.24.3.en: The reason for fearing men and not God is the saying of the Lord Christ: “For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (Jn 12:43). Fear of men may lead to denying the Lord Christ, as Peter did before the maid. It may also lead to a kind of lying, as Abraham did when he denied that Sarah was his wife (Gen 26:7).

29.24.4.en: * Why are you afraid, O Christians?

29.24.5.en: Christ speaks: “It is I; be not afraid.”

29.24.6.en: Why are you disturbed by these things? Why are you afraid?

29.24.7.en: I told you beforehand that these things would surely happen... “It is I; be not afraid. Then they willingly received him into the ship” (Jn 6:21).

29.24.8.en: When they knew Him and rejoiced, they were freed from their fears. “And immediately the ship was at the land whither they went.” An end was found at the land, from the region of water to the region of solid ground, from agitation to steadfastness, from the way to the goal.

29.24.9.en: St. Augustine * It is the will of God not to deliver you from fears, but to urge you to despise them, for this is greater than being delivered from them.

29.24.10.en: * What does this roughly mean? If the one who punishes me is a man, his punishments do not wholly condemn the one who falls under them. I can plead before him and prove to him that he is unjust, but because You are God this is impossible.

29.25.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Many seek the ruler’s favour; but every man’s judgment cometh from the LORD [26].

29.25.1.en: It is fitting for the believer to give honor to whom honor is due, and so to submit in a spirit of love, but not at the expense of his faith, remembering the great day of the Lord when he will enjoy his eternal rights. But if he fears men he seeks the face of the ruler, that is, the favor of his superior or master or ruler at the expense of his faith and the salvation of his soul.

29.26.0.en: An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked [27].

29.26.1.en: The righteous cannot bear the way of injustice, so he hates in the unjust man his violence and cruelty toward his brethren. And the wicked cannot bear the uprightness of the righteous man’s heart and conduct, because he feels that it condemns him and exposes his corruption, even if it does not confront him.

29.26.2.en: * The Apostle says: “What communion hath light with darkness?” Where there is a decisive contradiction, there can be no reconciliation between light and darkness. The person who shares in both together contributes nothing, because of their opposition and the contradiction of the one to the other at the same time in his common life. His faith extends the bright side, but his dark habits extinguish the lamp of the mind.

29.26.4.en: Turn my depths into a fountain of joy!

29.26.5.en: * Grant my heart to be enlarged with Your love, to rejoice in You, and to spring forth joy for others.

29.26.6.en: Let me bear the spirit of wise friendship, full of love.

29.26.7.en: Let my conduct carry neither excessive leniency nor exaggerated seriousness.

29.26.8.en: * Your Holy Spirit leads my life, and You rejoice in me as Your son.

29.26.9.en: Let me walk in the spirit of uprightness, and let Your righteousness reign over my life.

29.26.10.en: Let my hand not reach out to wrong, so that I desire no gift from anyone, and my mouth utters no word of flattery.

29.26.11.en: * I confess my weaknesses to You, but even if I fall I rise.

29.26.12.en: I do not give in to despair, but am filled with hope through Your Cross, O Forgiver of sins.

29.26.13.en: * My ears hear with You the sighs of my brethren, and my soul is poured out with them and cries out to You:

29.26.14.en: You are the hope of him who has no hope, You are the judge of the wronged and the suffering.

29.26.15.en: You are the Father of the fatherless, and the helper of those who have no one to inquire after them.

29.26.16.en: * Grant me the spirit of wisdom, so that I may be a peacemaker, and anger may not creep into my heart.

29.26.17.en: Rather let me rejoice in the peace of others, even of those who oppose me.

29.26.18.en: * Let me befriend Your children who love You, so that I learn much from them, and receive the blessing of their prayers for me.

29.26.19.en: Let me love even the wicked, and hate evil and abhor it.

29.26.20.en: Let me seek the salvation of the wicked, that they may enjoy the sweetness of fellowship with You.

29.26.21.en: * Let Your hand reach out to work in me.

29.26.22.en: For You are all love even in Your discipline.

29.26.23.en: Your rod and Your staff give me Your wisdom.

29.26.24.en: And Your firm care keeps me in Your bosom.

29.26.25.en: The enemy cannot snatch me from between Your hands.

29.26.26.en: * Your hand turns my heart from a tomb into a holy temple.

29.26.27.en: The enemy of good made of me a gloomy tomb.

29.26.28.en: Your Spirit turns me into a joyful heaven.

29.26.29.en: * Grant me true insight, so that I may see You, O Lover of all mankind.

29.26.30.en: Let me keep Your Law, for it is the delight of my heart.

29.26.31.en: It is my guide on the way of my pilgrimage.

29.26.32.en: * Be a keeper of my mouth and a guard of my lips.

29.26.33.en: So that I may be swift to hear, and deliberate in speaking.

29.26.34.en: * Grant me the spirit of humility, so that I may obtain Your mercy.

29.26.35.en: By humility the treasures of Your knowledge are opened to me.

29.26.36.en: By humility I enjoy Your wisdom.

29.26.37.en: By humility my face shines with Your light, and Your joy fills my heart.

29.26.38.en: By humility I find Your love and the love of my brethren sweet.

29.26.39.en: By humility Your Holy Spirit lifts up my heart, to enjoy its heavenly treasure.

30.0.0.en: 1 The words of Agur the son of the God-fearing woman of Massa. The oracle of this man to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal: 2 Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. 3 I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. 4 Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell? 5 Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. 6 Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. 7 Two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die: 8 Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: 9 Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain. 10 Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty. 11 There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother. 12 There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness. 13 There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up. 14 There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men.

30.0.1.en: The words of Agur the son of the God-fearing woman of Massa.

30.0.2.en: The oracle of this man to Ithiel.

30.0.4.en: We know nothing about Agur except what is mentioned in this chapter; we do not know his clan nor the tribe to which he belongs. As for Ithiel, a name whose meaning is “God is with me,” and Ucal, a name whose meaning is “the able,” perhaps they were friends of his, or two persons receiving instruction at his hands.

30.0.5.en: If we take the symbolic interpretation, the writer is Solomon the “Preacher,” the son of the godly David. And he writes a prophecy to everyone who wishes to be united with the Lord Christ as Immanuel, or God with us, or Ithiel, the Almighty, that is, Ucal. The repetition of the word Ithiel is to highlight the importance of the prophecy concerning the coming of Christ so that we may enjoy being with God. Perhaps its repetition points to His coming to the Jewish people as well as to the Gentiles.

30.0.6.en: As for the repetition of the name, mentioning it twice, it is because the number 2 points to love in the Holy Bible: the widow paid two mites, that is, she offered her whole heart; the good Samaritan paid two denarii to the innkeeper to care for the wounded man, that is, he offered his love; and in the sacrament of marriage the two become one by holy love. Thus we come to know the surpassing divine love by our union with the Almighty Savior Immanuel.

30.1.0.en: Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man [2].

30.1.1.en: Solomon the wise, who sought Wisdom as a companion for himself (Wis 8), feels the need of a constant thirst for her, so he counts himself a dull man, without understanding, until he enjoys perfect union with Wisdom.

30.1.2.en: * Ignorance is always accompanied by impetuosity, and leads people to attach great importance to their evil imaginations. Thus the victims of this disease think of themselves as great, and reckon that they are possessors of a knowledge which no one can attain. They seem to forget what Solomon says: “Be not wise in thine own eyes” (Prov 3:7), that is, according to your own individual judgment....

30.2.0.en: St. Cyril of Alexandria I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy [3].

30.2.1.en: In true humility Solomon the wise, as he stands before God the Holy One, feels that he has not yet learned wisdom, nor yet known the Holy One. And he remains so until he meets the Wisdom of God face to face and enjoys the vision of the Holy One in eternal glory.

30.2.2.en: The more a man enjoys wisdom, the more his longing for her increases, and he counts himself as one standing on the shore of wisdom, seeking to enter into its depths. From the intensity of his longing for her he thinks that he is dull, lacking in wisdom and very far from her.

30.2.3.en: * Thus Solomon was the wisest of all (1 Kgs 3:12), whether in his own days or before them, and God gave him largeness of heart, and an abundance of contemplation, more than the sand; for the more he entered into the depths of the great wisdom, the more he felt its great height. And he declared how wisdom is very far from him (Eccl 7:23).

30.2.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * It is not mere human wisdom that Solomon claims for himself, he who says: “God teaches me wisdom,” and also “All my words are from God,” ascribing to God everything he utters.

30.2.5.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended?

30.2.6.en: Who hath gathered the wind in his fists?

30.2.7.en: Who hath bound the waters in a garment?

30.2.8.en: Who hath established all the ends of the earth?

30.3.0.en: What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell? [4].

30.3.1.en: A wonderful question that Solomon the wise presents through the shadows, for he saw with the eye of prophecy the divine Word, the Wisdom of God who is in heaven, bowing the heavens and coming down to save man and to give him Himself. He is the One who in His discourse with Nicodemus said: “And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven” (Jn 3:13). And it was said of Him: “Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph 4:9-10).

30.3.2.en: That Heavenly One accomplished our salvation on the Cross and descended into Hades to bring up those who had died in hope, and to bring them in as captives into Paradise.

30.3.3.en: “Who hath gathered the wind in his fists?” Here he affirms His authority and His power to save, for He is the Almighty who gathers the wind as in His fists, and binds the water as in a garment, and establishes all the earth. Wherever man is found, whether in the air with the wind, or in the midst of the waters, or at the ends of the earth, God is able to gather him to Himself and care for him and accomplish his salvation. As the Lord Christ Himself says: “For God so loved the world... that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16).

30.3.4.en: As for his saying: “What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell?” the answer comes at the Incarnation of the Wisdom of God, who came to tell us of the surpassing mystery of the Father. He says: “The only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18), as He also says: “No man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Mt 11:27).”

30.3.5.en: * Do you believe that God sustains His creation and is able to do everything? Allow suitable works to follow your faith, and then He will hear you. Do not think of seizing the winds in the grasp of your hands, that is, of faith without works.

30.3.6.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian Every word of God is pure.

30.4.0.en: He is a shield unto them that put their trust in him [5].

30.4.1.en: The wise man affirms that every word of Scripture is pure and perfect because the Holy Bible is inspired by God (2 Tim 3:16). He who accepts it and trusts in it enjoys divine protection, and finds in its words a shield for his protection, a refuge and a fortress.

30.4.2.en: * The eating of bread is heaviness and sloth; but the word of life raises wings for the soul that it may fly with them.

30.4.3.en: St. Jacob of Serugh * He who trusts in the power of the Gospel trusts in God who makes it possible. He who has not received power from God cannot boast in the Lord, since he seeks his own glory.

30.5.0.en: Ambrosiaster Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar [6].

30.5.1.en: The words of God are perfect, they need no addition, they satisfy the soul and water it, and bring it into the divine glories. What we need is to enjoy the gift of a sound understanding of it.

30.5.2.en: * Nothing good comes from anyone other than God, especially the understanding of the Holy Scriptures.

30.5.3.en: * God guides those who listen to Him through the whole Holy Bible and through those who work, by means of his deepening.

30.5.4.en: * Although the whole Law is spiritual, the spiritual meaning is not known to all, but to those who have been given the grace of the Holy Spirit in the word of truth and knowledge.

30.5.5.en: * If you need the help of God at all times... we always need the Holy Spirit in order to understand the Holy Scriptures. Now is the time for Him to help me and show me the meanings of His words.

30.5.6.en: Origen * By accepting the Gospel a man becomes perfect after having walked according to the Law.

30.6.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die [7].

30.6.1.en: Remove far from me vanity and lies.

30.6.2.en: Give me neither poverty nor riches.

30.7.0.en: Feed me with food convenient for me [8].

30.7.1.en: Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say,

30.8.0.en: “Who is the LORD?” or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain [9].

30.8.1.en: What the wise man desires all the days of his life until the moment of his departure is to enjoy God Himself, so he does not ask for riches, lest his heart be occupied with them instead of the Giver of riches, and does not ask for poverty, lest because of his need he sin in one way or another. In other words, what occupies the wise man is his fellowship with the Holy One, and not riches nor poverty.

30.8.2.en: The believer fears to become like Jeshurun, of whom it was said: “But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deut 32:15). Rather he wishes to say of the Apostle Paul: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need” (Phil 4:11-12).

30.8.3.en: God alone knows what is suitable for each man, and what supports him in his salvation, for some are proved by the money which God gives them, so that they practice works of love and giving, and some are proved by need and by accepting it with thanksgiving and joy in the Lord.

30.8.4.en: Agur does not ask for riches nor poverty, not because they are evil, but lest he misuse them, for evil is in man’s conduct and his evil intention, and not in riches, nor in poverty.

30.8.5.en: * If riches and poverty are from the Lord, how can poverty or riches be evil?

30.8.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * Let the poor man be on his guard as well as the rich, for there are temptations for the man of poverty as for the man of wealth. As the wise man says: “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” He tells you how you can obtain these. It is enough for a man to have what is sufficient, because the rich man tends to burden his mind with cares and confusion, just as he fills his stomach with rich foods. Therefore the wise man asks to have what is necessary and suitable... to avoid the temptations of the world, so that the poor man may not despair, nor the rich man be haughty.

30.8.7.en: St. Ambrose * Solomon says: Give me neither poverty nor riches, give me only what is necessary and sufficient, “lest I be full, and deny thee,” and say: Who sees me? or being poor I steal and deny the name of my God; thus riches represent surfeit, and poverty represents the complete deprivation of the necessities of life, and sufficiency is a state of freedom from want and without excessive abundance. Sufficiency differs according to the bodily condition and present needs... Each condition needs special care to find a good table without exceeding the limits of real needs.

30.8.8.en: St. Basil the Great * Surely you see that this sufficiency is not desired for its own sake, but to secure the health of the body and clothing fitting to a man’s dignity, which allows a person to live with others respected and honored.

30.9.0.en: St. Augustine Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty [10].

30.9.1.en: It is fitting for the believer to take into account the circumstances of those with whom he deals, so that if a servant wrongs him he does not accuse him to his master, lest he deal harshly with him, and his soul groan within him, and his groaning reach the ears of God.

30.10.0.en: There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother [11].

30.10.1.en: The word “generation” here, as in the three following phrases, is meant to indicate a certain period of time, as the Lord Christ said of the Jews: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Mt 12:39).

30.10.2.en: Here the wise man warns us against insulting parents and not seeking their blessing.

30.10.3.en: The book of Proverbs often speaks of the family. When children walk in wisdom they bring joy to their parents (Prov 10:1; 15:20; 17:21, 25; 19:26; 23:24-25). It is a great disaster for children to lose their respect for their parents (Prov 23:22; 30:7), and to insult them (Prov 20:20), and to squander their money with bad friends (Prov 28:7; 29:3), and to rob their parents (Prov 28:24). Early discipline of children trains them to respect their parents and to appreciate parental love (Prov 13:24; 19:18; 22:15).

30.11.0.en: There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness [12].

30.11.1.en: He continues his discourse about the corrupt generation that insults parents and does not honor them, saying that it is a proud generation that does not look at its faults in order to be purified from them, but in a spirit of arrogance thinks that it is pure and better than the generation before it, that is, the generation of its parents.

30.11.2.en: * In any good work you do for your little brethren remember that your Master is the one who did it with them first. Listen and tremble, never take pleasure in your humility...

30.11.3.en: Perhaps this phrase provokes laughter in you, as though humility were calling you to be puffed up. Do not be astonished if humility makes you puffed up, for if this happens it shows that your humility is not genuine. How and in what way does this happen? When a man practices it to win the favor of men, not of God. When we practice it in order to be praised and counted great in the eyes of men. For this is from Satan.

30.11.4.en: Those who are puffed up because they are not proud please themselves by their humility and their high estimation of themselves...

30.11.5.en: Have you done a work that springs from humility? Do not boast of it, lest you lose all merit in it. For so it was with the Pharisee. He boasted of himself because he gave his tithes to the poor, and by this he lost the honor of the work. But it was not so with the tax collector, nor with Paul who said: “I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified.” He humbled himself by every means and was humble even when he had reached the summit...

30.11.6.en: When it occurs to your mind that you admire yourself because you are humble, remember your Master. Remember to what degree He humbled Himself, then you will not admire yourself nor ever praise yourself.

30.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up [13].

30.12.1.en: The secret of its not realizing its sins is that it is an arrogant generation that lifts up its eyes and its eyelids, that is, they speak with impudence in contempt of their parents and advisers, and even of the friends around them.

30.13.0.en: There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men [14].

30.13.1.en: The fruit of corruption and pride and contempt of others is the loss of divine grace, and the turning of the heart to extreme violence, so that they become like beasts of prey, their teeth deadly swords and their jaw teeth sharp knives. They practice their violence against the poor and needy who are unable to defend themselves.

30.14.s.en: 2. The two daughters of the horseleach

30.14.0.en: 15 The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough: 16 The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, It is enough. 17 The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it.

30.14.1.en: The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, “Give, give.” There are three things that are never satisfied.

30.14.2.en: Yea, four things say not, “It is enough” [15].

30.14.3.en: The horseleach (aluwqaah) means the bloodsucker. It is a voracious worm which eats and is not satisfied. Its two daughters are a symbol of its traits: it does not cease to suck blood without stopping. Perhaps the two daughters point to the love of money and the lust of the flesh.

30.14.4.en: Calmet sees that it points to greed, and that its two daughters are the love of money and covetousness.

30.14.5.en: Some see that it is the name of a woman who was known to him personally as well as to the public, and who had two daughters of bad reputation for their covetousness and corrupt morals.

30.14.6.en: Some rabbis see that the horseleach points to the fate and destiny that befalls man, or the inevitability of death, and that this fate and destiny has two daughters, the Garden of Eden and Gehenna, or Paradise and Hades. The first receives the righteous and the second the wicked.

30.14.7.en: Bochart also sees that the horseleach points to fate and destiny, and that its two daughters are the tomb and Hades, the first receiving the body at the death of man, and the second receiving the soul.

30.14.8.en: The Talmud sees that the horseleach points to Hades and that its two daughters are temporal authority and heresy.

30.14.9.en: Many of the Fathers of the Church see that the horseleach is understood to mean the authority of Satan.

30.14.10.en: He presents to us four things that are not satisfied, as symbols of the wicked heart, which deprives itself of God, the source of its satisfaction, so that whatever it asks and takes it remains in a state of emptiness and does not feel content. The wicked seeks money and bodily pleasures as two daughters that he embraces, but without satisfaction.

30.14.11.en: * The soul of man comes to vanity if it is occupied with the things of the world and concentrates on the needs of the body. Every day we wake up to eat and drink, and yet no one is satisfied so as not to hunger or thirst. After a short while we pursue gain daily and are seized by limitless greed, “the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing”! He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver... There is no limit to toil, nor profit in abundance... all things exist already and there is nothing new under the sun, but all is vanity.

30.14.12.en: St. Ambrose * Who can hide from himself what this riddle means? “The horseleach has three daughters, dear beloved ones, yet she is not satisfied, and with the fourth she is not satisfied when you say: Enough: the grave, and the love of a woman, and the earth that is not satisfied with water, and the fire that does not say, Enough.” The horseleach is the devil, and the daughters of the devil are dear and beloved, and they are not satisfied with the blood of the slain: the grave and the love of a woman and the dry earth and burning by heat.” He does not speak of a fornicator or a fornicatress, but of the love of a woman who is generally charged with being greedy. Remove it outside, and it bursts into a blaze of fire, abundantly; it is not satisfied; it makes a man’s mind feeble, and seizes all thought in order to feed lust.

30.14.13.en: St. Jerome * “The horseleach has three daughters, dear beloved ones.” Her daughters are presented to sin, daughters of fornication and murder and idolatry, these three do not satisfy her, for she is not satisfied. By destroying man with these deeds, sin does not change but grows continually. As for the fourth, she will not be persuaded to say Enough, that is, it is an unbridled lust... Just as the body is one and has many members, so sin is one, and contains within itself many lusts by which it casts its nets for men.

30.15.0.en: St. Hippolytus The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, “It is enough” [16].

30.15.2.en: A. Hades, which opens its mouth to swallow the dead, and will not stop doing so. It will not feel that it has been filled with the souls of the dead and so be content with those who have entered it. So the greedy man’s heart snatches up the love of money, and the more he obtains the more his thirst for more increases. St. Augustine likens him to one who suffers from dropsy: the more water he drinks the more he feels that he needs more without being satisfied. Or to one who drinks salt water which cannot quench the thirst of the thirsty.

30.15.3.en: B. The barren womb: perhaps he means by this the woman who loves evil with everyone and does not seek children, but seeks bodily pleasure; she will not feel that it is enough. Rather the practice of sin arouses her all the more.

30.15.4.en: Many a person thinks that he needs to practice the sinful bodily relationship in order to obtain satisfaction from it, but the truth is that it does not satisfy man’s needs but makes him thirstier for it, despite his feeling of distress after the sinful practice.

30.15.5.en: C. The sandy earth which absorbs water quickly, so that it is not fit for cultivation, but remains dry despite the rain that has fallen on it. So the love of money and bodily pleasures does not yield useful fruits.

30.15.6.en: D. The fire that does not say, “Enough”: whenever fuel is cast into the fire its flame increases, seeking to burn more and more, and the fire cannot feel a kind of contentment as long as fuel is cast into it.

30.16.0.en: The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it [17].

30.16.1.en: It is known of ravens and eagles that they attack their prey, whether a dead carcass or a living bird, by pecking at the eyes.

30.16.2.en: So he who despises his parents loses his inner insight and stumbles in the darkness; he cannot see the light of divine truth, nor enjoy the vision of the heavenly glories.

30.16.3.en: * “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth the old age of his mother,” that is, he who blasphemes God (his Father)... for the ravens coming from the caves pick out the eye of happiness.

30.17.0.en: 18 There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: 19 The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid. 20 Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have not done wickedness.

30.17.1.en: There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: [18]

30.18.0.en: The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid [19].

30.18.1.en: He tells us of the seriousness of adultery, that when a man falls into it once and again he feels that it is a natural bodily need, in which there is no sin. As the Scripture says: “They drink iniquity like water.” This is how some justify this sin, saying that it is a natural necessity like eating and drinking and sleeping, which a normal person cannot fail to practice.

30.18.2.en: The one who commits the sin thinks that no one has seen him, and that he gives no account for it. The Preacher concludes his book by saying: “For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil” (Eccl 12:14).

30.18.3.en: The wise man likens the position of the adulterer who does not care about what he commits to three examples: the way an eagle takes in the air, which no one can determine precisely, and the way of a serpent that goes upon a rock, and also the traces of a ship in the sea after it has passed; so the wicked man who commits sin tries to hide every trace of it, so that no one may trace it.

30.18.4.en: * If the house is founded upon a rock no harm will befall it. For there is no “way of a serpent upon a rock” (Prov 20:9)... The house falls if Christ is not its foundation. But the truly wise man builds his house upon a rock. This is the way in which the Lord built His Church upon the rock with a hedge and strength. This is the reason that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Mt 16:18). All the persecutions that come upon that house become as nothing. The house is built upon the rock.

30.18.5.en: Origen * Just as the serpent cannot leave a mark upon the rock, so Satan could not find sin in the body of the Anointed One. For the Lord says: “The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (Jn 14:30).

30.18.6.en: And just as the ship sailing in the sea leaves no trace behind it, so the Church which lives in the world as in a sea removes the hope that is upon the earth, for it keeps its life in heaven, and since it holds its way here for a short time, no one can follow its tracks...

30.18.7.en: “Three things are too wonderful for my understanding, and the fourth I know not: the traces of an eagle flying,” that is, the ascension of Christ, and the ways of a serpent upon a rock, that is, Satan finds no trace of sin in the body of Christ, and the ways of a ship crossing the sea, that is, the ways of the Church, which is in this life as in a sea, and which is directed by her hope in Christ through the Cross, and the ways of a man in his youth, that is, the ways of the One who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin.

30.18.8.en: St. Hippolytus * The gates of Hades cannot prevail against the rock upon which Christ builds the Church, nor against the Church, just as the way of a serpent upon a rock, according to what is written in Proverbs, cannot be found. Now if the gates of Hades have prevailed over anyone, such a one cannot be a rock upon which Christ builds the Church.

30.18.9.en: Origen Such is the way of an adulterous woman.

30.18.10.en: She eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith,

30.19.1.en: * This is the conduct of the Church which believes in Christ, for after committing adultery with the idols she renounced Satan, and was cleansed from her sins, and received forgiveness; then she affirms that she will not commit evil.

30.19.2.en: St. Hippolytus * “Such is the way of an adulterous woman; when she is washed she says: I have not done wickedness.” It is clear that this was said of her who was washed in the fountain, and does not remember the vices of her sins, but takes upon herself the virtue of preaching, and removes her stains with the living water, so that she no longer looks upon her sin, but rushes on in burning zeal. In a way she says that she does nothing evil now but has become an apostle of the truth, by forgetfulness she renounces her evil and preaches chastity through her consecration. This is the power of Christ the Lord, for even the sinner who is washed in His waters becomes renewed to virginity, and forgets what he did before. And by his new birth he proclaims the innocence of childhood, and does not know the sins of youth, and although he was formerly an adulterer because of the corruption of sin, he now becomes a virgin because of his faith in Christ.

30.19.3.en: Father Maximus, Bishop of Turin * Who is worthy to be burned now by this fire in his heart, so as not to be burned by it on the last day? I will describe to you who is the man who has this fire within his heart: imagine with me that two men each committed a sin of the same kind, say for example the most abominable kind of adultery. And that one of them felt after committing it no kind of remorse or grief or emotion about his sin, but as it was said in the book of Proverbs of the adulterous woman: “She eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have not done wickedness” (Prov 30:20). Look also at the second sinner; after committing his sin he could not bear it, and it was his conscience that punished and rebuked him, and he was tormented in his heart, unable to eat or to drink, fasting not by choice but because of the pains and torment of repentance. Imagine with me this man who “was bowed down to the end and went mourning all the day long, and his heart was filled with burning, and there is no health in his flesh” (Ps 38:6-7), and his sin does not cease to rebuke and reprove him. Compare this man with the first man who does not care about his sin and does not feel it: which of them do you prefer? Which of them, in your opinion, can have hope in the Lord? The man who repented of his sin is of course the one who has hope, for the more he is burned by the fire of punishment the more he becomes worthy of mercy. A period of punishment suffices him such as the Apostle Paul decreed for the man who committed adultery and then repented and grieved over his sin, because the punishment was beneficial to him, for the Apostle Paul imposed the punishment upon him, and when he saw that his grief was great and sufficient, he said: “Lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him” (2 Cor 2:7-8).

30.19.4.en: Let each one of us examine his conscience, and see what sins he has committed, so that when he knows that he ought to be punished, he may then ask God that the fire that came to Jeremiah, and also upon the two disciples at Emmaus, may come to him, so that he may not be delivered on the last day to the eternal fire, for if he sins here on earth and does not care about his sin and the divine fire does not work in him, his destiny in the end will be the eternal fire.

30.20.s.en: 4. Four things that cannot be borne

30.20.0.en: 21 For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: 22 For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with bread; 23 For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress.

30.20.1.en: For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: [21].

30.20.2.en: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with bread.

30.21.0.en: For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress [22].

30.21.1.en: * For three things the earth is disquieted (moved), that is, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. “And for four which it cannot bear,” that is, by the last coming of the Savior...

30.21.2.en: The disquieting of the earth means the changing of the things that are on the earth. Sin, which by its nature is a slave, reigned over the body of the mortal people. Truly, it reigned once in the days of the Flood, and again in the days of the people of Sodom, where it was not content with the land that was subject to it, but stirred up violence against strangers. And the third time in the case of hateful Egypt, for although it obtained Joseph who distributed food to all, lest they perish of famine, it did not repay his kindness well, but persecuted the children of Israel. The handmaid who is heir to her mistress is the Church of the Gentiles, for although she was a slave and a stranger to the promises, she drove out the free master, the synagogue of the Jews, and became the wife of Christ and His bride.

30.21.3.en: All the earth was moved by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the fourth it cannot bear. For He came first with the receivers of the Law, and second with the prophets, and third with the Gospel, where He declared Himself openly, and in the fourth He will come as Judge of the living and the dead, where all creation will not be able to bear His glory.

30.21.4.en: St. Hippolytus After presenting four examples of things which are hard to trace, he presents four others of hateful things which are hard to bear, to reveal that earthly man, although he loves sin and finds pleasure and attraction in it, cannot bear its consequences. These examples are:

30.21.5.en: A. A servant when he reigneth: perhaps he means the servant who betrays his master the king and assassinates him in order to occupy the throne of the kingdom. He had already likened him to the sweeping tempest and the sweeping rain (Prov 28:3). Kings in ancient times were often exposed to coups and assassinations, sometimes by one of their servants, as Eutropius attempted in the days of St. John Chrysostom.

30.21.6.en: It is often reported in history of people in lowly positions who, when they took over rule, became more violent than others. They wrong the poor and needy all the more, ignoring what they themselves had been.

30.21.7.en: B. A fool when he is filled with bread: that is, the poor and foolish man, when he obtains much of the good things, forgets his poverty, supposing that his sudden riches give him honor and authority over others.

30.21.8.en: C. An odious woman when she is married: this means one who was full of spite and desire for revenge, hated by all those around her. For if she marries, instead of rejoicing and being pleased with her husband so that they may live together in peace, she enters into disputes and strife with him and robs him of his peace.

30.21.9.en: D. An handmaid that is heir to her mistress: in the Septuagint it came: “A handmaid that has taken the place of her mistress.” Perhaps he means a maidservant who wins the affections of her master. For she uses every means to oppose her mistress and her children so that the master may divorce his wife and marry the maidservant and not care for his children. Thus ruin comes upon the family.

30.22.0.en: 24 There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: 25 The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; 26 The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks; 27 The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands; 28 The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings’ palaces.

30.22.1.en: There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: [24].

30.22.2.en: He presents a third set of four examples marked by wisdom despite their small size and man’s contempt for them, and they are:

30.22.3.en: * Four are the smallest on the earth, and they are wiser than the wise: the ants have no strength, yet they prepare their meat in the summer. In the same way the Gentiles prepare for themselves eternal life by faith in Christ with good works. The conies are a feeble folk, and make their houses in the rocks. And it can be said that the Gentiles are built upon Christ, the spiritual Rock, who becomes the cornerstone. The spider, which feeds itself with its hands, and can be easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of the rich, meaning that the thief, with his hands stretched out on the cross, rested on the cross of Christ, and dwelt in Paradise, the stronghold of kings: the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The locusts have no king, and yet they move in orderly ranks as under one leader. The Gentiles have no king, for sin reigned over them, and now that they believe in God they are engaged in a heavenly battle.

30.23.0.en: St. Hippolytus The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer [25].

30.23.1.en: A. The ant: despite its smallness it is marked by diligence and care for the future with precise order and collective work. Ants store food in the summer so as to find food in the winter. So it is fitting for man to be diligent in his daily work as in his spiritual life, for what he does today supports him tomorrow.

30.23.2.en: God provides the ant with its food, but on its part it is bound to work diligently.

30.23.3.en: So it is fitting for the Church to work together under the leadership of the invisible Head, in a spirit of love and unity, without divisions or strife (1 Cor 3:3; 1:10).

30.23.4.en: * Be prudent and provide yourself with what is in the future in heaven. Be wise, and follow the ant, as the Scripture says: “Store up in the summer, lest you hunger in the winter.” The winter is the last day, the day of tribulation, the winter is the day of transgressions and bitterness. Gather what can be found for you in the future. If you do not do so you will perish, being neither prudent nor wise.

30.24.0.en: St. Augustine The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks [26].

30.24.1.en: B. The coney: according to the Law it is reckoned among the unclean animals because it chews the cud, but does not part the hoof (Lev 11:5). It is a small animal resembling the rabbit and of its size, and because its round feet are soft it cannot dig a hole for itself, so it takes refuge in the rock, sheltering in it (Ps 104:18). It points to the sinful man, for he cannot establish for himself a refuge in which to hide, but he must hide in Christ the true Rock (1 Cor 10:4), and so find rest and satisfaction and peace.

30.24.2.en: * Here (Solomon) points to those who have no strength, and yet store up treasures for eternal life by their good works... And the rock is in truth the refuge of the coney that lives in it. He says: You also, though you are weak, run toward the rock of true faith, and by it you recover life.

30.24.3.en: The man who enjoys works enters the Kingdom. Therefore he says: Do not despair of the Kingdom of Heaven because of the weakness of your faith, but believe in the promises, hasten to the works that you have been commanded. Christ is the Lion, and in truth all rational beings are reckoned a flock in relation to Him. (Jeremiah) says: “I am a child” because of the natural lightness of movement; it was said of the lion that he walks without hindrance.

30.24.4.en: St. Didymus the Blind * It befits the mind to cleave to this phrase continually, and so be strengthened by its constant use and unceasing meditation on it, and in this way drive away from itself all other rich thoughts, disdaining them... content with the poverty of this single phrase. And thus it reaches with the utmost speed the beatitude mentioned in the Gospel, which occupies the first place among the beatitudes, for He says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 5:3).

30.24.5.en: And when a man becomes exceedingly poor with such poverty, the saying of the prophet is fulfilled in him: “Let the poor and needy praise thy name” (Ps 74:21). Truly what poverty is greater than for a man to know of himself that he has no strength with which to defend himself, seeking daily help from the generosity of another. And so he knows that every moment of his life depends on divine providence... and so he cries out to the Lord daily: “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me” (Ps 40:17).
